strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: using multi-modal panoramic renderings (RGB + lifted semantic features + range) as an explicit 2D-3D interface allows direct reuse of pretrained 2D VLMs (CogVLM-17B) with only lightweight modifications (zero-conv adapters), addressing both the language-comprehension and 3D-generalization limitations of traditional 3DVG models.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on ScanRefer (61.0 single-dataset, 62.0 S+R) and Nr3D (74.6/76.1, +4.7% over prior art), competitive on Sr3D, with a fair comparison protocol that groups methods by training regime (single vs. mixed dataset).

Comprehensive generalization analysis beyond standard benchmarks: cross-dataset transfer to ARKitScenes+SceneVerse and 3RScan+RIORefer with substantially smaller degradation than baselines, and a novel text-perturbation protocol (rephrase, affordance, affordance-no-name, mask) showing large gains (+15.9 on Aff.†, +8.5 on Mask.) where lexical class matching is unavailable.

Convincing representation-level validation: Table 4 shows panoramas outperform all non-oracle pinhole view-selection strategies (41.3-51.0 vs. 61.0), with the gap widening as more objects are referenced, and even surpassing the GT-target pinhole oracle for 4+ object queries - this directly supports the core claim about 360-degree context.

Thorough ablations and supplementary material: modality/loss/QA ablations (Tab. 5), camera placement factors (Tab. 6, Figs. 7-8), test-time augmentation analysis, adapter initialization, mesh vs. 3DGS scene representation, runtime analysis (3.3s/query on A100), and extensive qualitative figures. Limitations and future work are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on privileged evaluation settings in parts of the experiments: Table 2 (cross-dataset) and Table 3 (text variants) use ground-truth object segmentation (and sometimes GT semantic labels) for all methods, so absolute numbers and even the claimed generalization gaps may differ under predicted proposals; while this is applied uniformly to baselines, the practical open-vocabulary claim is only partially validated.

Strong input assumptions: the method requires a renderable 3D representation (mesh or 3DGS) with known camera parameters, offline precomputed semantic feature fields (multi-view DINOv2 lifting), and camera placement tied to raw capture trajectories - these may not hold for many real 3DVG deployment scenarios and are somewhat underexplored.

Test-time setup is costly relative to baselines: inference requires ~9.6 VLM forward passes per query (2.4 cameras × 4 yaw rotations) plus SAM-based lifting and multi-view fusion (~3.3s/query on an A100); the paper reports runtime honestly but does not compare inference cost against supervised baselines, and the TTA gains partly inflate comparisons.

Component novelty is modest and largely assembled from existing techniques (zero-conv adapters from ControlNet, EMD/Wasserstein digit loss from EMO, SAM, DINOv2 features); the paper's contribution is primarily in the representation design and system integration rather than new learning methodology. The individual gains from the adapter, EMD loss, and geometric QA are small (ablation deltas of ~0.3-3 points).

Some evaluation protocol choices raise questions: text variants are generated by LLaMA 3.3 without human verification of semantic preservation; the two-stage variant details for ReferIt3D are relegated to the supplementary; the view-dependent split analysis on panorama equivariance is not deeply analyzed despite panoramas being orientation-agnostic (VD gains are achieved but the mechanism could be clearer).

Fine-tuning on the target benchmark (ScanRefer/ReferIt3D) with a 17B VLM means the 'state-of-the-art' comparison against much smaller specialized models partly reflects backbone scale; an equal-capacity control or discussion of this confound is missing.

strengths: The core idea—multi-modal panoramic renderings as an explicit 2D–3D interface for pretrained VLMs—is clean, well-motivated, and conceptually simple: it preserves 360-degree object-to-object relations, removes the need for view-direction prediction, and avoids task-specific fusion heads, which is a meaningful design contribution even if the individual components are not novel.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on ScanRefer (61.0 single-dataset, 62.0 mixed) and Nr3D (+4.7 over prior art in single-dataset setting), with comparisons properly grouped by training regime (single vs. mixed dataset) for fairness.

The generalization analysis is a genuine strength relative to much of the 3DVG literature: cross-dataset transfer to ARKitScenes and 3RScan (Table 2, with baselines re-run under GT segmentation to isolate 3D generalization) and a thoughtfully designed text-perturbation protocol (Table 3) showing large gains precisely when explicit class cues are removed (+15.9 on Aff.†, +8.5 on Mask), supporting the claim that the method reasons rather than lexically matches.

The panorama-vs-pinhole study (Table 4) directly validates the central representational claim with a controlled comparison including an oracle upper bound, and the finding that panoramas exceed the pinhole oracle for relation-heavy queries is convincing evidence that 360-degree context matters.

Supplementary material is unusually thorough: camera placement ablations (Table 6, Figs. 7–8), test-time augmentation analysis, adapter initialization ablation, mesh-vs-3DGS comparison with runtime analysis, prompt templates, and training curves—this level of transparency supports reproducibility.

The multi-modal feature adapter (zero-initialized injection of geometric/semantic features into ViT layers) and the EMD loss over digit distributions are reasonable, lightweight technical contributions with ablation support (57.5 -> 58.4 for EMD).
weaknesses: The method requires a renderable 3D representation (mesh or 3DGS) as input, plus a full offline preprocessing pipeline (RANSAC floor estimation, feature lifting, panoramic rendering). This limits applicability to raw point cloud settings that most 3DVG baselines operate on, and the paper does not clearly discuss this deployment constraint in the main text.

Inference efficiency is a real concern: 3.3 seconds per query with ~9.6 VLM forward passes (17B backbone, LoRA fine-tuned), which is far heavier than typical 3DVG models and limits practicality for the robotics/embodied applications the introduction motivates. A latency/budget comparison against baselines is absent.

On Sr3D, the method is not SOTA (79.1 vs. VGMamba 81.3 single-dataset; 79.9 vs. UniVLG 81.7 mixed), and on ScanRefer the margin over prior work is modest (61.0 vs. 60.0). The SOTA claim is accurate for ScanRefer/Nr3D but should be stated more carefully as benchmark-dependent.

The fine-tuned CogVLM-17B backbone makes several comparisons arguably unfair: zero-shot VLM methods (SeeGround, VLM-Grounder) use frozen/API models, and some gains over 3D-specific models may stem from backbone scale rather than the panoramic interface. An ablation varying the backbone (e.g., a smaller grounding-capable VLM) would substantially strengthen the attribution of gains to the framework itself.

The abstract and conclusion gesture at 'open-vocabulary' grounding, but no open-vocabulary evaluation is performed; all benchmarks use closed label sets and (for generalization/text experiments) GT object segmentation. The claims and evidence are not fully aligned here.

Some design elements are under-justified: why EMD with these specific place-value weights, why mid-level vs. late-layer injection points for geometric vs. semantic features (stated but not ablated), and the synergy claim between geometric features and geometric QA rests on a 0.8-point difference (60.2/60.7 vs. 61.0) with no variance or significance reporting anywhere in the paper.

Single-run results with no error bars, and several ablation gaps within ~1 point, make it difficult to judge which component claims are statistically meaningful. This does not undermine the main results but does weaken some of the finer-grained conclusions.

The method assumes multiple-target/no-target queries are out of scope and excludes non-visible ground-truth samples during training; while stated, these scope restrictions are somewhat buried and deserve more prominent discussion given the 'generalizable framework' framing.

strengths: The core idea—using multi-modal panoramic (equirectangular) renderings as an explicit 2D–3D interface for pretrained VLMs—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly articulated; it neatly sidesteps view-direction prediction and the narrow-field limitations of pinhole-based VLM approaches.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: state-of-the-art results on ScanRefer and Nr3D under both single- and mixed-dataset regimes, plus dedicated generalization experiments on unseen 3D datasets (ARKitScenes+SceneVerse, 3RScan+RIORefer) and LLM-generated text perturbations, with baselines re-run under matched conditions (GT segmentation) for fairness.

The ablation program is unusually thorough: panorama vs. multiple pinhole configurations (including an oracle, showing the panoramic advantage grows with the number of referenced objects), modality/objective ablations, camera-placement factor analysis, adapter initialization, test-time augmentation saturation, and mesh vs. 3DGS scene representations.

Well-designed technical components: zero-initialized feature adapters preserve pretrained VLM behavior, and the EMD-based digit loss is a sensible way to make autoregressive box-coordinate prediction numerically aware; visibility-aware multi-view fusion provides a principled mechanism to filter unreliable per-view predictions.

The supplementary material is substantive and supports reproducibility: prompt templates, hyperparameters, runtime analysis (3.30s/query on an A100), camera-placement details, and honest discussion of failure modes (e.g., 3DGS artifacts) and limitations.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a strong, specific backbone (CogVLM-17B with LoRA) makes it hard to disentangle the contribution of the panoramic representation from the raw capability of modern VLMs; an ablation with a smaller/older VLM backbone would clarify how much the representation itself matters.

Several headline comparisons use ground-truth object segmentation/masks (Tables 2, 3, and the two-stage variant), which is fair for controlled comparison but means some generalization claims are not fully end-to-end; the gap between GT-mask and detected-object performance is not quantified in the main pipeline.

Inference cost is notable: ~9.6 VLM forward passes per query (2.4 cameras × 4 test-time rotations), with TTA alone contributing a large fraction of accuracy (54.8 → 61.0 in Fig. 9); this inflates the effective compute and complicates comparison against single-pass supervised baselines.

The method requires a renderable 3D representation (mesh or 3DGS) plus known camera geometry, precomputed multi-view feature fields, and SAM at inference; applicability to raw point clouds or real robot-captured scenes without clean reconstruction is untested, and mesh-based performance degrades noticeably with 3DGS inputs (74.6 vs. 71.2 Nr3D).

The EMD loss (Eq. 3) is effectively a weighted L1 expectation over digit distributions—simple and useful but a modest technical contribution; likewise, the camera-placement score is a heuristic combination of hand-crafted factors, and the ordering of Eq. 1 with ε=1e-3 could be stated more carefully.

Not fully state-of-the-art everywhere: UniVLG and VGMamba exceed the proposed method on Sr3D (81.7 vs. 79.9; 81.3 vs. 79.1), and the paper would benefit from a more direct analysis of why template-based spatial language is relatively weaker.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated idea: using panoramic (equirectangular) renderings as an explicit 2D–3D interface that leverages pretrained 2D VLMs while preserving scene-wide context, avoiding the viewing-direction problem of pinhole-based approaches.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art or top-2 performance on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer under both single-dataset and multi-dataset training regimes, with a carefully constructed, fair comparison (methods grouped by training data, marked where datasets differ).

Convincing evidence that the panoramic representation itself (rather than just backbone capacity) drives the gains: the panoramic-vs-pinhole study (Tab. 6) shows large gaps over non-oracle pinhole baselines that widen with the number of referenced objects, and the zero-shot comparison (Tab. 2) shows the pipeline beating GPT-4V/Qwen2-VL-72B-based methods with a much smaller CogVLM-17B.

Comprehensive generalization analyses: cross-dataset evaluation on ARKitScenes+SceneVerse and 3RScan+RIORefer with GT proposals to isolate scene generalization, and a thoughtful text-perturbation protocol (Para., +Aff., +Aff.−N, Mask) showing large gains when lexical cues are removed (+15.9, +8.5).

Thorough ablations covering EMD loss, semantic/geometric features, geometric QA, camera placement factors, adapter layer placement, zero-init adapters, test-time rotations, and backbone scaling (Tab. 4 shows a 7B variant outperforming LLaVA-3D on accuracy, memory, and latency).

Practical deployability evidence: a fully automated COLMAP+3DGS variant (55.1 Acc@0.25) and an end-to-end demonstration on a self-captured iPhone video with per-stage time/memory accounting; failure modes and limitations (reconstruction noise, slower inference) are honestly discussed.
Well-written, well-organized manuscript with good figures and a detailed supplementary that supports reproducibility (prompts, hyperparameters, two-stage variant details).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: individual components are largely borrowed from prior work (zero-initialized conv adapters from ControlNet, DINOv2 feature lifting as in LIFT-GS/SpatialRGPT-style pipelines, digit-token box regression from CogVLM, EMD loss from EMO). The contribution is primarily a well-executed system rather than a new algorithmic principle.

Compute considerations are not fully matched against baselines: the main results rely on CogVLM-17B with LoRA fine-tuning, four yaw-rotated test-time augmentations, and ~2.4 panoramic views per scene (~9.6 forward passes/query at 3.3 s each), whereas most compared 3D methods are far cheaper at inference; a compute-matched comparison against strong supervised baselines would strengthen the SOTA claim.

Main results use mesh-rendered panoramas derived from curated ScanNet meshes, which are cleaner than the raw point clouds used by prior 3D baselines; although the 3DGS/automated variants in the supplementary mitigate this concern, the headline SOTA numbers are achieved under a favorable input condition that is disclosed but kept out of the main tables.

Generalization experiments use GT object segmentation for all methods, which simplifies the setting; results with predicted segments for at least one baseline configuration would make the transfer claims more complete.

Some design decisions are weakly justified by ablations: adapter layer placement yields essentially identical accuracy across configurations (60.9–61.0), and the geometric contribution is small (masking at inference drops accuracy only 61.0→60.5), suggesting the pipeline's gains come mostly from the VLM plus semantic features; there is also a minor inconsistency between the main-paper ScanRefer overall (61.0) and the supplementary mesh result (61.6) that is not clearly reconciled.

The method inherits a heavy offline pipeline (COLMAP ~87 min, 3DGS ~43 min, semantic feature lifting ~24 min per scene) and 80 GB CPU usage, which limits applicability despite the paper's practical framing; this is acknowledged but only partially quantified against the benefit.
Evaluation on a single self-captured scene for real-world deployment is anecdotal; a larger set of in-the-wild captures would better substantiate the practical-use claim.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: using panoramic renderings as an explicit 2D-3D interface allows direct reuse of a pretrained 2D VLM with only lightweight zero-conv adapters, sidestepping heavy 3D token engineering (contrast with Scene-LLM, Chat-Scene, LLaVA-3D).

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art or near-top performance on ScanRefer and Nr3D under both single-dataset and multi-dataset training regimes, with a sensible grouping of baselines by training data to keep comparisons fair.

Unusually thorough generalization analysis: cross-dataset transfer (ARKitScenes+SceneVerse, 3RScan+RIORefer) and four LLM-generated text perturbation variants, showing large robustness gains exactly where class-name cues are removed (+15.9 on +Aff.-N).

Well-designed ablations covering camera placement scoring factors, modality contributions, EMD loss, geometric QA, adapter placement (with layer probing), zero-init, and test-time rotations; a dedicated panorama-vs-pinhole study including an oracle baseline convincingly demonstrates the benefit of the 360-degree field of view.

Practical deployment evidence beyond benchmarks: fully automated COLMAP+3DGS variant (55.1 without GT meshes/trajectories), backbone scalability with latency/memory numbers, and an end-to-end demo on a self-captured iPhone video.
Honest limitations section acknowledging reconstruction dependence, latency relative to feed-forward 3D methods, and restricted query types.
weaknesses: Dependence on offline 3D reconstruction is a substantive limitation relative to the paper's framing: headline results use ground-truth (human-cleaned) meshes; the fully automated 3DGS variant drops to 55.1 and excludes 49/141 validation scenes where COLMAP fails, which weakens the claim of relaxing the high-quality 3D input requirement.

The zero-shot comparison in Table 2 is not fully equitable: PanoGrounder's zero-shot setting still assumes a clean 3D reconstruction, multi-modal feature rendering, and its panoramic pipeline, whereas zero-shot baselines (SeeGround, VLM-Grounder) operate under weaker input assumptions; the input conditions differ across rows.

Generalization experiments (Tables 3-4) are conducted with GT object segmentation (and sometimes GT semantic labels) for all methods, which isolates the effect nicely but limits how directly the conclusions transfer to the fully automatic setting.

Computational profile is heavy: CogVLM-17B requires 51.6 GB GPU memory and 3.3 s/query online, plus hours of offline reconstruction (COLMAP 87 min + 3DGS 43 min); the paper acknowledges this but the headline configuration is far from real-time robotics use.

Several design choices are heuristic rather than principled (camera-placement score balancing coverage, clearance, and trajectory distance; axis-aligned box fitting; view-dependent left/right reasoning must rely on yaw-rotation TTA), and the sensitivity to equirectangular distortion is analyzed but not resolved.

The distance-to-trajectory factor requires a prior capture trajectory, so the placement strategy has a mandatory and an optional component whose behavior in the truly trajectory-free case is underexplored.

Reproducibility is plausible given detailed hyperparameters and prompts, but the pipeline spans many components (COLMAP, 3DGS, DINOv2 lifting, SAM, CogVLM+LoRA); no code release is stated, and full replication would be demanding.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated intermediate representation: using multi-modal panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface for pretrained VLMs is a simple yet effective idea that sidesteps view-direction prediction and preserves scene-wide context, clearly differentiated from pinhole-based VLM methods and 3D-token-based MLLM approaches in the related work.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on Nr3D (+4.7 over ViewSRD in the single-dataset setting) and best ScanRefer Overall/Multiple scores, with fair grouping of baselines by training regime (single vs. multi-dataset) and a transparent two-stage variant for candidate-based evaluation.

Comprehensive generalization analysis beyond standard benchmarks: cross-dataset evaluation on ARKitScenes+SceneVerse and 3RScan+RIORefer with re-run baselines under GT-segmentation-controlled conditions, plus a thoughtful LLM-generated text-perturbation suite (Para/+Aff/+Aff.-N/Mask) that isolates reasoning ability from lexical matching; the +15.9 gain on +Aff.-N is a particularly convincing signal.

Persuasive evidence that panoramas (not backbone capacity) drive gains: the pinhole-vs-panorama study (Tab. 6) showing panoramic views surpass even a pinhole oracle for relation-heavy queries, the zero-shot comparison against GPT-4V/Qwen2-VL-72B-based methods with a 17B backbone, and the backbone scalability study (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B) in the supplement.

Unusually thorough supplementary material: ablations on camera placement factors, adapter layer placement (with ViT probing to justify the design), zero-initialized adapters, test-time rotation counts, mesh vs. 3DGS representations, a fully automated COLMAP+3DGS pipeline, per-category/elevation analyses, and an end-to-end deployment on a raw iPhone-captured scene with runtime/memory breakdowns. Limitations are honestly discussed.

Training is well-engineered: automatic generation of image-text-box supervision via rendered instance-ID maps avoids manual 2D annotation, and the EMD-style digit loss plus auxiliary geometric QA are cheap, sensible additions validated in the ablation.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on large pretrained components and nontrivial pipelines: CogVLM-17B, DINOv2 feature lifters, SAM, COLMAP+3DGS reconstruction, and mesh cleaning. The headline results use GT meshes; the practical 3DGS variant degrades (61.6 to 60.8, and 55.1 fully automated on a reduced 92-scene subset), so the claimed robustness to casual captures is only partially quantified.

Computational cost at inference is nontrivial: ~9.6 VLM forward passes per query (2.4 cameras x 4 TTA rotations) and 3.3 s/query at 17B. The paper should clarify how the 2.4x reported 'independent inference' TTA gain interacts with the visibility-aware aggregation and whether gains hold without TTA.

Component novelty is largely incremental: zero-conv adapters (ControlNet), EMD/EMO-style digit losses, DINOv2 feature lifting, and multi-view fusion are established techniques recombined; the main novelty is the panoramic interface and camera placement scoring. This is acceptable for an Algorithms/General contribution but means the scientific case rests heavily on the empirical evidence, which mostly holds up.

Some evaluation asymmetries: baseline results were re-run by the authors under GT-segmentation settings, and several baseline cells are missing (e.g., BUTD-DETR/MCLN on 3RScan due to implementation restrictions); minor inconsistency between the main-paper ScanRefer number (61.0) and supplementary Ours(Mesh) (61.6) suggests different evaluation subsets and should be clarified. The EMD loss's +0.9-1.0 gains are modest relative to the abstract's emphasis.

Assumption of a floor-plane structure and axis-aligned bounding box fitting limits applicability to multi-floor or heavily rotated-object scenes, and the two-stage variant for ReferIt3D leans on benchmark-provided GT candidate segments for selection-level comparisons, which slightly weakens the end-to-end story on those benchmarks.

Generality of the 'generalization' claim: ScanNet/ARKitScenes/3RScan are all indoor, furniture-scale datasets with similar object vocabularies; claims of generalizable 3DVG would be better supported by an outdoor or cross-modality test, though this is acknowledged in future work.
